screens.title: Match Conditions in Junos Routing Policies
screens.subtitle: Craft precise 'from' statements using prefix-list, route-filter, protocol, AS-path, and community matching.

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how Junos uses the 'from' statement inside a policy term to identify which routes a term applies to. Match conditions are the core of policy logic: they let you pick routes by prefix, protocol, AS path, community, neighbor, interface, or next hop. That granularity is what allows predictable redistribution, export filters, and selective advertisement. For example, a prefix-list gives you exact matching and reuse; a route-filter adds operators like 'orlonger' and 'prefix-length-range' to match ranges of prefix lengths. Matching by protocol, such as OSPF versus BGP, prevents you from accidentally importing routes from the wrong source. AS-path regular expressions let you target routes by their AS sequence, and community matches let operators tag and then filter traffic with precise intent. We will also cover common mistakes: unintentionally ANDing conditions inside a single 'from' block and misinterpreting 'orlonger'. By the end of this chapter you will be able to write terms that safely accept, reject, or tag routes and verify their effect in a test environment. Consider a simple use case: accept only OSPF-learned internal networks while rejecting certain external BGP prefixes; this chapter shows how to achieve that cleanly and test it.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A routing policy term matches only when all conditions in a single 'from' block are true. Use separate terms to express OR logic and choose prefix-list or route-filter depending on whether you need exact or range-based prefix matching.

content.html:

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Match Conditions — What they control and why they matter

You will learn how each 'from' match filters routes, when to use prefix-list vs route-filter, and how protocol, AS path, and community matches give you operational control.

In this lesson
Precision filters, prefix tools, AS path regex
Concept map
prefix-list
Exact named prefixes for reuse across policies.
route-filter
Range and length-based operators like orlonger and prefix-length-range.
AS-path & community
Regex matching and tagged route attributes for granular control.
Quick note
Remember: conditions inside a single 'from' block are ANDed. Use separate terms to express OR logic.
Key Takeaway

Choose prefix-list for exact matches and route-filter for ranges. Plan your terms to avoid accidental ANDing of unrelated conditions.

Coming up

Exact lists vs flexible filters for subnets.
AS path & regex

Orientation

This chapter focuses on the practical mechanics of 'from' statements. Watch the examples, then try the hands-on exercise to define prefix-lists, write route-filters, and apply an export policy to a BGP group.

No CLI interactivity here — code is shown for study and replication in a lab.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure and verify a range of 'from' match conditions in Junos routing policies. First, you will define and reuse prefix-list entries so the same named prefixes can be referenced from multiple policy terms. This reduces duplication and simplifies auditing. Second, you will use route-filter operators such as exact, orlonger, and prefix-length-range to match prefix ranges and control which prefix lengths are included. Third, you will match routes by protocol, AS path regular expressions, and BGP community attributes, which lets you implement controlled redistribution and peer-specific filtering. Finally, you'll understand how to combine match conditions correctly: when conditions inside a single 'from' statement are ANDed, and how separate terms create OR logic. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic and a verification step so you can test your configuration in a lab. A common misconception we clear up here is that multiple conditions in one 'from' do not create OR logic; they require all conditions to be true. These objectives map directly to the hands-on exercise where you'll build a policy using both prefix-list and route-filter and verify results after applying it to a BGP group.

keyIdea.title: Objective summary
keyIdea.text: Master prefix and attribute matching, use route-filter operators for ranges, match protocol/AS path/community values, and combine terms correctly to express OR logic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Verification & Mistakes
screens.subtitle: How to test and avoid common misconfigurations

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on verification steps and common pitfalls. You will learn to apply a policy to a BGP export and then inspect the advertising table to confirm only intended prefixes are sent to a neighbor. The verification sequence includes committing the configuration, using show policy-options and show route advertising-protocol to compare before and after state, and checking policy hit-counters if available. You will also learn typical mistakes: using orlonger where an exact match was required, writing AS-path regex that unintentionally matches more AS numbers than intended, and putting multiple unrelated match types into one 'from' block which results in no matches. Each objective card includes a short mnemonic and a verification micro-step so you can check competence quickly in a lab. Emphasizing verification prevents outages caused by over-broad rejects or accidental advertisement. By learning both how to write and how to verify policies, you'll be able to reason about policy effects and recover quickly if a filter behaves unexpectedly. Try the provided hands-on exercise to practice these verification steps in a safe test environment.

keyIdea.title: Verification focus
keyIdea.text: Always test policies by applying them in a controlled peer group, inspect advertising-protocol output, and use separate terms to express OR logic to avoid unintended empty matches.

Verify and avoid common mistakes

Verification helps you confirm policy effects and catch syntax or logic errors early.

Verification steps
Commit, run show policy-options, apply to a BGP group, then show route advertising-protocol neighbor to compare advertised prefixes.
Common mistakes
  • Using orlonger when exact match was intended.
  • Placing unrelated conditions in one 'from' block, creating impossible ANDs.
  • Incorrect AS-path regex that overmatches prefixes.
Quick lab checklist
  1. Define prefix-list and route-filter entries.
  2. Create policy-statement terms that accept intended routes.
  3. Apply policy to a test BGP group and observe advertised routes.
  4. Adjust and re-verify until results match expected lists.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

screens.title: The 'from' statement explained
screens.subtitle: How match conditions determine whether a term applies to a route

narration.text: The 'from' statement is the selector in a Junos policy term; it defines the conditions a route must meet to trigger the term's actions. Think of it as a filter composed of one or more match attributes. Each 'from' block is evaluated as a logical AND: every condition inside that block must be true for the route to match. If you need OR behavior — for example, accept routes from either AS 65001 or AS 65002 — you must create separate terms, each with its own 'from'. A concrete example: a term that has 'from { protocol ospf; prefix-list INTERNAL_NETS; }' will match only OSPF-learned routes whose destination exactly matches an entry in INTERNAL_NETS. A common misconception is to expect multiple 'from' lines to behave like OR; they do not. Another important practical point is ordering: policy-statement terms are evaluated top to bottom, so place more specific match terms before broader catch-all terms. For verification, use 'show policy-options' to inspect configured prefix-lists and 'show route advertising-protocol' to see which prefixes would actually be advertised after applying an export policy. To summarize: define precise match conditions, use separate terms for OR, and order terms to avoid premature matches. What specific set of conditions will you need to express in your next policy?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A 'from' block is a set of match conditions evaluated as an AND; use separate terms to express OR, and order terms from specific to general.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › From Statement
What 'from' does

A 'from' block lists attributes a route must match. All attributes inside the block must be satisfied for the term to trigger.

Example match
from { protocol ospf; prefix-list INTERNAL_NETS; }
This matches only routes learned from OSPF that are exactly listed in INTERNAL_NETS.
Misconception
Multiple 'from' lines are not OR. To express OR, use separate terms.
Key Takeaway

Design terms for clarity: AND inside 'from', OR via multiple terms, specific before general.

Visual: term evaluation (card-first)
Term: MATCH_INTERNAL_OSPF
from { protocol ospf; prefix-list INTERNAL_NETS; } then accept
Only routes that satisfy both protocol and prefix-list are accepted.
Ordering note
Place narrow matches first. A broad reject term at the top can prevent later specific accepts from executing.

screens.title: Prefix-list: exact matching and reuse
screens.subtitle: Named lists for exact prefixes and configuration reuse

narration.text: A prefix-list is a named collection of exact prefixes defined under policy-options for reuse across multiple policy-statement terms. It is the right tool when you need precise control over which exact destinations are matched, and when those prefixes are stable or maintained by a team. For example, defining INTERNAL_NETS once and referencing it from several match terms prevents duplication and simplifies updates. A concrete configuration example shows the structure and how a term references it. One common mistake is expecting prefix-list to match more specific subnets; it does not. If you need to match a subnet range or include more specific prefixes, use route-filter with orlonger or prefix-length-range instead. When verifying, ensure that the prefix entries are correct and that the term references the exact list name. Also be mindful of ordering: prefix lists used in a top-level accept term will be applied before less specific route-filters. Practice creating a prefix-list, referencing it from a term, committing, and verifying the policy with show policy-options and show route advertising-protocol to see the actual advertised prefixes. This gives you the confidence that only the intended exact prefixes are used in policy decisions.

keyIdea.title: Prefix-list use
keyIdea.text: Use prefix-list for exact prefix matches and reuse. It will not match more specific prefixes unless those exact entries are listed.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Prefix-list
Define and reuse prefix-list

Prefix-lists contain exact prefixes. Reference them from a term's 'from' to create precise matches.

Configuration example
policy-options {
    prefix-list INTERNAL_NETS {
        172.16.0.0/16;
        192.168.100.0/24;
    }
}

policy-statement FILTER_AND_TAG {
    term MATCH_INTERNAL_OSPF {
        from {
            protocol ospf;
            prefix-list INTERNAL_NETS;
        }
        then accept;
    }
}
Concrete example
If OSPF has learned 192.168.100.0/24, the term will match. 192.168.100.128/25 would not match unless listed explicitly.
Common mistake
Expecting prefix-list to match descendants. Use route-filter orlonger for that behavior.
When to use prefix-list
  • Exact control of a small, managed set of prefixes.
  • When multiple policies need the same prefix set — reuse the named list.
  • When you need minimal risk: only explicitly listed prefixes are matched.
Key Takeaway

Use prefix-list for explicit, reusable exact matches. For subnets or ranges, prefer route-filter.

screens.title: Route-filter: range and length operators
screens.subtitle: Understanding orlonger, prefix-length-range, and upto semantics

narration.text: Route-filter gives you flexible prefix matching beyond exact entries. The most used operators are exact, orlonger, and prefix-length-range. exact matches only the specified prefix, similar to a single prefix-list entry. orlonger matches the specified prefix and any more specific prefixes — so 10.0.0.0/8 orlonger would match /8 and any /9, /16, /24 under that block. prefix-length-range lets you bound matches to a specific length window; for example, route-filter 172.16.0.0/16 prefix-length-range /24-/32 will match only prefixes inside 172.16.0.0/16 with masks between /24 and /32. A common confusion comes from upto: it matches the specified prefix and less specific prefixes up to a given length, which is often the opposite of what an operator expects. Use prefix-length-range when you need a minimum prefix length. For IP ranges across a major network, route-filter with prefix-length-range is more accurate than attempting contiguous ranges with through. Concrete example: to accept only customer subnets between /16 and /24 inside 10.0.0.0/8, use prefix-length-range. Remember also that route-filter is configured directly inside the term, not always as a reusable named list, though you can replicate patterns for consistency. Always test with your routing table to verify which actual prefixes match the filter.

keyIdea.title: Operator summary
keyIdea.text: Use exact for a single prefix, orlonger to include more specific subnets, and prefix-length-range to bound allowed mask lengths precisely.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Route-filter Operators
Operator comparison

Choose the operator that expresses the prefix set you actually want to match.

exact
Matches only the prefix exactly as written.
orlonger
Matches the prefix and any more specific prefixes beneath it.
prefix-length-range
Specify a mask length window, e.g., /8-/24, to precisely control allowed masks.
Concrete examples
route-filter 10.0.0.0/8 orlonger
route-filter 172.16.0.0/16 prefix-length-range /24-/32
First matches any prefix inside 10.0.0.0/8 of any longer mask. Second matches only /24 to /32 prefixes within 172.16.0.0/16.
Gotcha: upto
upto matches less specific prefixes and is often the opposite of the desired behavior when you want more specific matches.
Key Takeaway

Pick route-filter operators that match the prefix-mask semantics you need; test in a routing table before committing to production.

screens.title: Protocol matching and use cases
screens.subtitle: Match routes by their origin protocol to control redistribution and export

narration.text: Matching by protocol is a simple but powerful technique: you can target routes based on whether they were learned by BGP, OSPF, direct, static, or another protocol. This is useful when redistributing between protocols or when crafting export lists. For instance, an export policy might accept only direct routes and routes learned from OSPF, while rejecting BGP-learned routes to avoid advertising certain external networks. A concrete scenario: you have internal OSPF networks you want to advertise to a BGP peer but you do not want to advertise external BGP-learned prefixes. In that case, a term with 'from { protocol ospf; prefix-list ADVERTISED_PREFIXES; }' ensures only OSPF prefixes are considered for advertisement. Misconceptions often arise when administrators assume protocol matches imply stable route ownership; protocols can change after reconfiguration so verification is key. The process for applying this match is: define the prefix or filter, write a term that includes the protocol condition, apply the policy to the BGP export, commit, and then inspect advertising-protocol output. Always test in a lab or with a controlled peer to validate the behavior before rolling out broadly.

keyIdea.title: Protocol match
keyIdea.text: Use protocol matching to restrict a policy to routes learned by a particular routing protocol, making redistribution and export behavior explicit and verifiable.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Protocol Matching
When to match by protocol

Control redistribution and exports by explicitly matching the route's origin protocol.

Use case
Advertise only OSPF-learned internal prefixes to a BGP peer while suppressing externally learned BGP prefixes.
Process
  1. Define prefix-list or route-filter for intended prefixes.
  2. Create term with from { protocol ospf; ... } then accept;
  3. Apply as export policy on BGP group and verify advertising output.
Key Takeaway

Protocol matching isolates a route's source, enabling precise redistribution decisions and safer exports.

Example term
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term OSPF_ADVERTISE from protocol ospf
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term OSPF_ADVERTISE from prefix-list ADVERTISED_PREFIXES
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term OSPF_ADVERTISE then accept
After applying this as an export to a BGP peer, only OSPF-learned prefixes listed in ADVERTISED_PREFIXES will be sent.

screens.title: AS-path matching with regular expressions
screens.subtitle: Target routes by the Autonomous Systems they traversed

narration.text: AS-path matching uses regular expressions against the AS path attribute to identify routes based on their AS traversal. This is especially useful in BGP policies where you want to accept or reject routes from specific origin ASes or patterns of transit. For instance, the pattern ".* 64500$" matches AS paths that end with 64500, indicating the route came from that AS or originated there. Another common pattern is '^64500.', which matches routes that begin with 64500 then have at least one more AS, useful when you want to match routes that originated in a given AS and were then passed on. A typical pitfall is writing regexes that are too broad and unintentionally matching multiple AS sequences; test regexes against sample AS paths before applying them. In practice you often place an as-path match together with protocol bgp in the 'from' block so you only evaluate AS paths for BGP routes. Always verify with route output to see the AS paths present and consider using a dedicated test peer to avoid accidental route acceptance. As a closing thought: AS-path regex is powerful, but it demands careful testing — a small pattern mistake can alter which prefixes you accept or reject.

keyIdea.title: AS-path
keyIdea.text: Use AS-path regex to target routes by origin or traversal, but verify patterns carefully to avoid unintended matches.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › AS-path Matching
Regex examples and guidance

AS-path matching is applied to BGP routes and uses regex to match AS sequences in the path attribute.

Examples
as-path ".* 65000$"  # ends with 65000
as-path "^64500 ."  # starts with 64500 then at least one more AS
Combine with 'protocol bgp' in the 'from' block for clarity and safety.
Misconception
A regex that is too permissive can match unintended AS sequences. Test against actual AS-path values before committing.
Key Takeaway

AS-path regex gives precise control over BGP route selection. Validate patterns using real AS-path samples to prevent mistakes.

Concrete scenario
You want to accept only routes that originated in AS 64500. Use as-path "^64500$" to match paths that are exactly that AS. If you want routes that passed through 64500 last, use ".* 64500$".

screens.title: Community matching and named communities
screens.subtitle: Tagging routes and matching those tags in policies

narration.text: BGP communities are arbitrary tags attached to routes and can be matched in policies for fine-grained control. You define named communities under policy-options and give them members such as 'no-advertise' or numeric values like 65000:100. After tagging routes — for example, via another policy that sets a community — you can match those communities in a 'from' block to accept, reject, or modify route treatment. A concrete example in the chapter defines COMMUNITY CUSTOMER_A_ROUTES as member 65000:100 and then matches it inside a term to accept those routes. Communities are particularly useful when you need to mark traffic for selective export or when peers use communities to indicate special handling. Misconceptions include thinking communities are globally consistent; they must be agreed upon with peers and documented. Also, community attributes can be modified by transit providers, so verify the community values visible in your routing table before relying on them in a policy. A common operational approach is to tag internal routes with a local community and then match that community when building export filters to peers. Community matching and named communities means define and use named communities to tag routes you want to recognize later. document community semantics with peers and verify values in the routing table.. In practical terms, tagging routes and matching those tags in policies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Community use
keyIdea.text: Define and use named communities to tag routes you want to recognize later. Document community semantics with peers and verify values in the routing table.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Community Matching
Tag and match with communities

Communities let you mark routes and later select them in policies based on those tags.

Config snippet
policy-options {
    community CUSTOMER_A_ROUTES members 65000:100;
}

policy-statement FILTER_AND_TAG {
    term MATCH_BGP_COMMUNITY {
        from { protocol bgp; community CUSTOMER_A_ROUTES; }
        then accept;
    }
}
Practical notes
  • Agree community semantics with peers to ensure consistent tagging.
  • Use communities to selectively export or to prevent advertisement to certain peers.
  • Verify community values in the route table before relying on them in policies.
Key Takeaway

Communities are flexible tags; define, document, and verify before using them as policy selectors.

screens.title: Neighbor, interface, and next-hop matching
screens.subtitle: Match by adjacency and forwarding attributes

narration.text: Other handy 'from' match conditions include neighbor, interface, and next-hop. Matching by neighbor is typically used with BGP to apply policies specific to a peer. For example, you may accept certain prefixes only from a particular neighbor IP or AS. Matching by interface makes sense for direct routes tied to specific physical or logical interfaces; if a route is known via a specific interface, you can selectively accept or reject it. Next-hop match is useful when the next-hop value encodes a path decision you want to use in policy. A real-world example: treat routes learned from an internal fabric interface differently from those learned on a WAN interface. Misconceptions include expecting neighbor-based matches to replace AS-path checks; neighbor addresses are precise but do not capture AS sequence. Use neighbor matches for peer-specific handling and AS-path for origin/transit pattern matching. When combined correctly with prefix or community matches, neighbor/interface/next-hop selectors let you create precise per-peer or per-link policies that reflect operational intent. Always test changes in a controlled environment so you can confirm that the match attributes observed in the routing table align with your expectations.

keyIdea.title: Adjacency matches
keyIdea.text: Use neighbor for peer-specific rules, interface for locally connected routes, and next-hop for forwarding-based selections; combine them with other matches for precision.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Neighbor & Interface Matches
Peer and adjacency selectors

These matches are concrete and precise: neighbor matches a specific peer, interface matches routes learned on an interface, next-hop matches the forwarding neighbor.

Use neighbor to
Apply policies that only affect traffic from a particular BGP neighbor IP.
Use interface to
Identify locally attached routes and control them by ingress interface.
Concrete example
A term with from { neighbor 192.0.2.1; route-filter 10.0.0.0/8 orlonger; } then reject; will reject 10.0.0.0/8 prefixes from that specific neighbor only.
Key Takeaway

Neighbor/interface/next-hop matches are precise tools for peer- or link-specific policies. Combine them with other matches for richer intent.

screens.title: Combining match conditions: AND vs OR
screens.subtitle: How to express complex logic using terms and multiple 'from' statements

narration.text: Combining match conditions correctly is essential to avoid unintended behavior. Inside a single 'from' block all conditions are ANDed; the route must satisfy each listed attribute. To express OR logic — for example, accept routes from AS 65001 OR AS 65002 OR routes in a prefix range — you must create separate terms, each with its own 'from'. Each term is evaluated independently and the policy processes terms from top to bottom until a match occurs or the policy ends. For example, three terms can each match a different AS-path or one term can match a route-filter while another matches a prefix-list. A common error is placing two protocols in a single 'from' block such as 'from { protocol bgp; protocol ospf; }' which will never match because a route cannot be both at the same time. When designing combined logic, plan for explicit fall-through behavior — add a catch-all reject term at the end if you want explicit denial rather than implicit deny. To verify logic, simulate or inspect policy hit counters if supported and test with representative routes. In short, design terms to map to the OR/AND logic you need and place them in the proper order to capture specificity first.

keyIdea.title: Logic rules
keyIdea.text: Inside 'from' is AND; separate terms create OR. Order terms to evaluate specific matches before broad ones and add an explicit catch-all if desired.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › AND vs OR
Expressing OR logic

Use separate terms to express OR; one term per alternative makes intent explicit and testable.

Example: three-term OR
term T1: from { as-path "65001"; } then accept; term T2: from { as-path "65002"; } then accept; term T3: from { route-filter 10.0.0.0/8 prefix-length-range /16-/24; } then accept;
Mistake to avoid
Putting multiple unrelated conditions in one 'from' expecting OR behavior; this creates impossible ANDs that never match.
Ordering and catch-all
Place specific accepts above broad rejects. If you prefer clarity, add a final CATCH_ALL_REJECT term with then reject to make intent explicit rather than relying on implicit deny.
Key Takeaway

Map the logic you need to term structure: AND inside from, OR via multiple terms, ordered from specific to general.

screens.title: Apply a policy: prefix-list + route-filter demo
screens.subtitle: Define lists, create terms, apply as BGP export, and verify advertising output

narration.text: This walkthrough ties together prefix-list and route-filter in a short hands-on scenario. First, define a prefix-list ADVERTISED_PREFIXES with two exact prefixes you want to advertise. Next, create an export policy with two terms: one that accepts OSPF routes from that prefix-list, and a second that accepts direct routes using a route-filter with orlonger for 172.16.0.0/16 orlonger. Finally, apply the policy to a BGP group as the export policy and commit. Verifying involves running show policy-options to confirm your lists and show route advertising-protocol to see which prefixes are being advertised. In the provided example configuration we accept OSPF-learned exact prefixes and direct routes in the 172.16 network hierarchy. A common verification pitfall is forgetting to apply the policy to the BGP group or misnaming the prefix-list. When you test, use test peers or a lab so you can observe advertising-protocol changes without impacting production. Practicing this flow — define lists, write terms, apply policy, and verify — will make these match conditions second nature. Apply a policy: prefix-list + route-filter demo means define prefix-list, write policy-statement terms combining protocol and filters, apply as export on a bgp group, then verify with show route advertising-protocol.. In practical terms, define lists, create terms, apply as bgp export, and verify advertising output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Define prefix-list, write policy-statement terms combining protocol and filters, apply as export on a BGP group, then verify with show route advertising-protocol.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Hands-on Demo
Starter configuration
set policy-options prefix-list ADVERTISED_PREFIXES {
    192.168.10.0/24;
    192.168.20.0/24;
}

set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term OSPF_ADVERTISE from protocol ospf
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term OSPF_ADVERTISE from prefix-list ADVERTISED_PREFIXES
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term OSPF_ADVERTISE then accept

set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term DIRECT_ADVERTISE from protocol direct
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term DIRECT_ADVERTISE from route-filter 172.16.0.0/16 orlonger
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term DIRECT_ADVERTISE then accept

set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_POLICY term REJECT_ALL_OTHERS then reject
Apply to BGP group and verify
set protocols bgp group EXTERNAL_PEER neighbor 172.16.1.2 set protocols bgp group EXTERNAL_PEER export EXPORT_POLICY
After commit, verify with: show policy-options; show route advertising-protocol bgp 172.16.1.2
Key Takeaway

Follow the flow: define lists, compose terms, apply to peer, verify advertising. Small mistakes are found quickly when you verify expected advertisements.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting tips
screens.subtitle: Debugging policies and testing your match logic

narration.text: Troubleshooting routing policy match conditions often comes down to three practical checks: verify the configured match attributes, confirm the actual route attributes in the routing table, and simulate or observe the policy's effect on advertised routes. First, check that prefix-lists and route-filters are spelled and referenced correctly; a misnamed prefix-list will silently not match. Second, inspect protocol, AS-path, and community values in the route entries because match attributes come from the route itself. For AS-path regex mistakes, test patterns against sample AS-path strings to ensure your expression matches only intended sequences. Third, ensure you applied the correct policy to the intended BGP group or export point; forgetting to attach an export policy is a frequent operational oversight. Use explicit final terms like CATCH_ALL_REJECT if you want to make implicit deny behavior clear in the policy. When debugging, apply policies in a lab or to a test peer and use show route advertising-protocol to compare before and after. A final tip: add temporary accept terms scoped narrowly to validate selectors before enabling broader rejects. This staged approach reduces risk and helps you incrementally verify that match conditions do exactly what you intend.

Debug checklist

  • Inspect route entries for protocol, AS-path, and community values used in matches.

Practical tip
Stage changes: start with narrow accept terms to confirm matches, then add broader rejects. Use an explicit reject term at the end to document denial behavior.
Common Mistake

Putting unrelated match types together expecting OR logic. That yields no matches and unexpected policy results.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points you should remember. First, prefix-list provides exact, reusable prefix matching and is suitable when you need strict control over specific networks. Second, route-filter adds powerful operators such as exact, orlonger, and prefix-length-range to match prefix ranges and enforce mask-length constraints. Third, protocol, AS-path, community, neighbor, interface, and next-hop matches let you shape policy behavior by route origin, traversal, tags, and adjacency. Fourth, remember logical rules: conditions inside one 'from' are ANDed and separate terms implement OR. Finally, always verify: apply policies to a test peer or group, use show policy-options and show route advertising-protocol to confirm intended results, and validate AS-path regex against sample paths. These ideas combined give you precise control over which prefixes are accepted, rejected, or advertised. Keep these concepts in mind as you design policies that are both safe and maintainable.
